records.sourceFile: Readiness to train - Return to baseline strength and velocity following strength and power training.pdf

paper.citation: Vernon A, Joyce C, Banyard HG. Readiness to train: return to baseline strength and velocity following strength or power training. Int J Sports Sci Coach. 2020;15(2):204-211.
paper.abstract: The study tracked the return to baseline of back-squat mean and peak velocity, 1RM and countermovement jump peak velocity over 96 h after a strength-oriented session and a power-oriented session in strength-trained men. Velocity at 60% 1RM and above was meaningfully reduced at 24 and 48 h after the strength session and had recovered by 72 h, while 1RM and jump measures did not change meaningfully. The authors conclude that velocity monitoring may be a more practical guide to full recovery and readiness to train than 1RM or jump testing.
paper.tldr: After a heavy back-squat session, the authors report bar speed at 60% 1RM and above stayed below baseline at 24 and 48 h and was back by 72 h, while 1RM and jump peak velocity showed no meaningful change at any time. Velocity may be a more sensitive readiness check than 1RM or a jump test, though this rests on one protocol in 14 to 15 men.
paper.methods: Repeated-measures crossover study in which strength-trained men completed a strength session (five sets of five at 80% 1RM) and a power session (six sets of three at 50% 1RM) in random order, one week apart. After a baseline 1RM and load-velocity profile, back-squat mean and peak velocity, 1RM and countermovement jump peak velocity were measured at 24, 48, 72 and 96 h using a linear position transducer. Cohen's d of 0.60 or more was treated as a meaningful change from baseline.
paper.findings: The authors report moderate reductions in mean and peak velocity at 60%, 80% and 90% 1RM at 24 and 48 h after the strength session, no meaningful change at 72 or 96 h, and only trivial to small velocity changes after the power session. Maximal strength (1RM) and countermovement jump peak velocity showed only trivial to small changes at all times after either session. The effect-size flags in Tables 1 and 2 do not fully match this text: several 24 h strength-session reductions are flagged large, peak velocity at 80% 1RM is flagged medium at 72 h, and velocity at the 1RM load is flagged medium to large at several points after the power session.
paper.limitations: The sample is small, all male, and studied with one back-squat protocol, so findings do not apply to other lifts or to athletes without this training history. The authors state the countermovement jump may not be sensitive enough to detect strength-session fatigue. The abstract gives the power session as three sets of six and 14 participants, the Methods six sets of three and 15 recruited, and the table effect-size flags conflict in places with the text's summary of which changes were meaningful.
paper.practicalImplications: After a heavy strength session, a coach could delay heavy (60% 1RM and above) velocity-based work until about 72 h, and check bar speed at fixed loads before loading rather than relying on 1RM or jump tests. The study does not show that velocity checks improve later training results.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Bar speed at 60% 1RM and above recovered by 72 h after a heavy back-squat session, so coaches could use a fixed-load velocity check to decide when to repeat heavy lower-body work. The study did not test whether timing heavy work this way improves later strength gains.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The men had no current musculoskeletal injury and the study did not include injured athletes, so it cannot inform return to sport. It cannot show that velocity recovery signals readiness after injury.

records.sourceFile: Recovery and Performance in Sport-                        Consensus Statement .pdf

paper.citation: Kellmann M, Bertollo M, Bosquet L, Brink M, Coutts A, Duffield R, et al. Recovery and Performance in Sport: Consensus Statement. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2018.
paper.abstract: Recovery and fatigue and their effect on performance were reviewed at an international symposium in 2016. The statement defines central terms, describes how recovery and fatigue can be assessed, outlines training-recovery-performance models, and gives recommendations on monitoring training and recovery and on individualising recovery activities. It also identifies important questions for future research.
paper.tldr: Recovery and fatigue should be monitored as a continuum, using several measures rather than one, and recovery should be planned as part of training. The statement stresses that the value of many monitoring tools and recovery methods is still unclear, so athletes need individualised decisions.
paper.methods: Consensus statement from an invited international symposium on recovery and performance, held at the Technical University of Munich Science and Study Center Raitenhaslach in September 2016. Experts from several disciplines discussed definitions, frameworks and practical implications, and the statement summarises the current knowledge. The text does not describe a formal consensus or evidence grading process.
paper.findings: The statement treats recovery and fatigue as a continuum, with underrecovery, non-functional overreaching and overtraining syndrome as possible outcomes of an imbalance. It advises assessing recovery against the demands of the sport, using performance measures where possible and recognising that proxy tests are often used. It recommends monitoring both external and internal load and using change criteria such as the smallest worthwhile change or Z-scores. It notes that single measures show only one aspect of recovery, so combined physiological and psychological measures are advised. It says short-term recovery interventions can help during heavy training, but their long-term effect on performance is unknown, and that cold water immersion results conflict, with some studies reporting blunted resistance-training adaptations. It also reports that coaches tend to overestimate athletes' need for recovery.
paper.limitations: This is expert opinion with no new data and no described grading of evidence. The authors say the regular-use value of markers such as creatine kinase and urea nitrogen is unclear and that the use of blood lactate is debated. The text is the accepted manuscript, so volume, issue and page numbers are not printed, and the year is taken from the copyright line.
paper.practicalImplications: Plan recovery around the season phase, the type of stress (muscle damaging, mentally fatiguing or metabolically demanding) and the competition schedule, rather than adding fixed recovery treatments after every session. Monitor with a small set of measures chosen for validity and reliability, combine performance, physiological and psychological data, and judge changes against each measure's typical error. Reduce load before competition to dissipate fatigue.
paper.athleteDev: Programme recovery as a planned part of training, for example recovery microcycles and tapers before competition, and match the method to the stress. Use psychological strategies after mentally fatiguing work and recovery aimed at soreness after high muscle-damage sessions. Avoid routinely using short-term recovery methods such as cold water immersion in blocks where resistance-training adaptation is the goal, since the statement notes that these may blunt adaptation.
paper.rtp: The statement does not address injury rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria. It can inform how recovery and readiness are monitored in athletes, but it gives no validated thresholds for clearing an athlete to play after injury or illness.

records.sourceFile: Recovery following the extra-time period in soccer - Practioner perspecties and applied practices.pdf

paper.citation: Field A, Corr LD, Thompson CJ et al. Recovery following the extra-time period of soccer: practitioner perspectives and applied practices. Biol Sport. 2022;39(1):171-179.
paper.abstract: An online survey of soccer practitioners explored perceptions and practices for recovery after matches that go to extra time (ET). Of 72 included practitioners, 63 (88%) believed ET delays recovery, and 49 (68%) reduced training loads and intensities for up to 48 hours after ET matches. Inductive content analysis identified five themes: conditioning, player monitoring, recovery practices, training and future research. Practitioners ranked tracking physiological and physical responses, nutritional interventions to accelerate recovery and changes in acute injury risk as the most important research areas.
paper.tldr: Most soccer practitioners think extra time slows recovery and adjust training and recovery for up to 48 hours afterwards, but practice varies widely and the surveyed approaches have not been tested for effectiveness. Monitoring player responses after extra time is a clear research priority.
paper.methods: Online survey sent to 208 club and federation representatives between January and June 2020, with 87 returned and 72 complete responses analysed. The survey had 14 main questions with sub-items, using 5- and 7-point scales, rankings and open-ended questions. Frequencies were calculated for closed items, and open responses were coded inductively by two researchers. The survey followed the CHERRIES reporting checklist.
paper.findings: Eighty-two percent agreed that practices should be adapted after extra time compared with a 90-minute match, and 88% agreed that extra time delays recovery. Conditioning for extra time was not standard: 49% said they did not condition players outside peak periods, 36% did and 15% sometimes did. Seventy-two percent allowed players to return to training based on fatigue markers after extra time. Training loads and intensities were adapted by 46% at 24 hours, 68% at 24 to 48 hours and 39% at 48 to 72 hours. Common adaptations included longer cool-downs, extra rest days, changes to carbohydrate and protein intake, and longer or more intense massage and cold-water immersion.
paper.limitations: The sample is convenience-based and self-selected, with a 42% response rate and possible bias towards this topic because respondents knew it in advance. Most respondents worked in English leagues and at professional level (44 of 72), and the instrument was not validated. The results describe perceptions and reported practice, not measured recovery, so the paper cannot show that any adapted practice improves recovery or reduces injury.
paper.practicalImplications: Most surveyed practitioners reduced training loads and intensities for up to 48 hours after extra time and used fatigue markers to return players to training, which gives a common reference point for planning. The survey does not show which choices work, and the authors note that longer cool-downs have shown no effect on muscle soreness or glycogen resynthesis, so use player monitoring data to judge any adaptation.
paper.athleteDev: Some practitioners prepared for extra time with longer training matches or a load increase 4 to 5 days before a knockout match, but the authors judge that such short-term preparation is unlikely to produce the needed adaptation. After extra time, practitioners commonly limited high-speed running, accelerations and decelerations in drills for the next 24 to 48 hours. The paper does not show that any of these steps improve recovery or readiness.
paper.rtp: The study does not address rehabilitation or return to sport after injury, and no injured players were studied. It describes how uninjured players were returned to training after extra-time matches, so it cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria. Injury risk after extra time is named as a research priority, but this paper does not measure it.

records.sourceFile: Recovery management in sport - Overview and outcomes of a nine-year multicenter research program.pdf

paper.citation: Wiewelhove T, Schneider C, Kellmann M, Pfeiffer M, Meyer T, Ferrauti A. Recovery management in sport: Overview and outcomes of a nine-year multicenter research program. Int J Sports Sci Coach. 2024.
paper.abstract: The REGman project (2012 to 2021) aimed to advance understanding of recovery management in elite sport. It used a two-stage framework: first, investigating monitoring measures for short-term fatigue and recovery, and second, assessing recovery interventions, including psychological strategies, sleep, cooling, heating, compression, active recovery, stretching, massage and foam rolling. Recovery interventions had inconclusive or marginal group-level effects with possible individual differences. Individualised reference ranges improved classification accuracy compared with group-based ranges.
paper.tldr: Across nine years of work, recovery interventions produced mostly small or uncertain group-level effects, so the authors put training planning, sleep and nutrition first. They recommend monitoring individual responses over time, with individual reference ranges for blood markers, before adding recovery strategies.
paper.methods: Research note linking the outputs of a nine-year, two-phase multicentre programme funded by the German Federal Institute of Sport Science. The authors list 65 publications (original research, reviews and meta-analyses) mapped to project modules, outline the conceptual framework, and summarise the main findings on monitoring and recovery interventions. No systematic search is described.
paper.findings: In the first phase, a diagnostic inventory of monitoring measures found acceptable sensitivity to change in several self-report, performance-based and physiological measures during short overload microcycles, with the ARSS and SRSS developed and validated. Changes in monitoring measures correlated poorly with performance changes. In the second phase, the recovery interventions showed low to trivial statistical evidence of effect at group level, although some athletes may benefit more than others. A Bayesian approach using individual reference ranges for creatine kinase and urea improved classification accuracy compared with group-based ranges. The authors also note that regular cold water immersion may attenuate strength and muscle gains after resistance training, so it should be avoided straight after strength or hypertrophy sessions.
paper.limitations: The paper is an overview by the programme's own investigators and does not describe a systematic search or appraisal. It gives no per-study sample sizes or effect sizes, so the conclusions cannot be checked here. The authors state that monitoring changes did not reliably predict performance outcomes, and that individual response patterns need replicated measurement, which is hard to do in elite settings.
paper.practicalImplications: Put training planning, sleep and nutrition ahead of recovery products. Monitor individual responses over time with repeated measures, use individual reference ranges when interpreting blood markers, and treat changes in monitoring data as a prompt to review training. Use recovery interventions as optional additions once the basics are in place, matched to the type of stress.
paper.athleteDev: During strength or hypertrophy blocks, avoid cold water immersion or cryotherapy straight after training sessions, since the authors note it may blunt gains, and reserve it for competition or intensified periods where it is needed. Use sensitive monitoring tools such as the ARSS, SRSS, submaximal tests and individually referenced blood markers to decide when to adjust load.
paper.rtp: The programme studied recovery and monitoring after training and competition loads, not injury rehabilitation or return to sport, so it does not provide return-to-play criteria. Because the authors report uncertain group-level effects for most recovery interventions, the findings should not be used as a basis for clearing an injured athlete to play.

records.sourceFile: Recovery practices in Division 1 collegiate athletes in North America.pdf

paper.citation: Murray A, Fullagar H, Turner AP, Sproule J. Recovery practices in Division 1 collegiate athletes in North America. Phys Ther Sport. 2018;32:67-73.
paper.abstract: This study established current recovery practice and attitudes in 152 Division 1 collegiate athletes across basketball, American football and soccer, using an online questionnaire. Sleep, cold water immersion and nutrition were perceived as the most effective modalities. CWI was the most used modality, and only 24% of athletes both believed in and used sleep as a recovery method. The authors conclude that there is a discrepancy between perception and use of recovery modalities in collegiate athletes.
paper.tldr: Collegiate athletes rate sleep as the most helpful recovery method, yet only about one in four both believes in it and lists it as a recovery practice, while cold water immersion is the most used method. Most athletes said they chose methods on evidence and experience together, and only 5% cited evidence alone.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional online survey of 152 student-athletes (men's basketball n=10, men's American football n=116, women's soccer n=26) at a North American Division 1 university, from 161 invited (94% response), completed over two months in 2016. The 16-item questionnaire covered demographics, current practice after training and competition, beliefs about 8 modalities rated on a 5-point scale (coded as benefit or not), and the basis for choices. Group differences used chi-square, ANOVA or t tests, and clustering was used to group athletes by modality choice.
paper.findings: Sleep had the highest overall rating (4.54 out of 5; 87.5% believed it helps), followed by CWI (83.6%) and nutrition (79.6%). Over half (53.9%) did not believe compression helps. CWI was the most used modality after training (55.9%) and competition (65.8%), and stretching was next. Sleep was used by 22.4% after training and 20.4% after competition. Among all athletes, 24.3% believed in and used sleep, 63.2% believed in sleep but did not list it as a recovery practice, and 65.1% both believed in and used CWI. Also, 65.1% believed in nutrition but did not list it as a recovery practice. Athletes chose their methods on evidence and experience together (74%), and 59% judged recovery by how they felt. The number of modalities used did not differ between post-training and post-competition.
paper.limitations: The study uses self-reported beliefs and use, with no objective measure of modality use or effect. The sample comes from one institution and three teams, with more than three-quarters from American football, and the authors say a larger sample is needed to examine differences between sports. The sleep item may have been interpreted as night sleep only, so naps may have been missed. The abstract describes a 16-item questionnaire while the methods describe 17 questions.
paper.practicalImplications: Collegiate staff should not assume that athletes who value sleep are using it as part of recovery, so sleep education deserves attention alongside other modalities, as the authors recommend. Because CWI is the most used modality despite what the authors describe as mixed support in the literature, staff can review why it is being used. Staff should also check whether athletes who believe in nutrition for recovery are putting that belief into practice.
paper.athleteDev: Sleep was rated the most helpful method but listed as a recovery practice by fewer than a quarter of athletes, so sleep education and planning are a low-cost target; the authors suggest schedules and academic stress may limit sleep but call this speculative. The paper notes that CWI is used widely even though its benefits for team sport performance appear small, so its use should be a deliberate choice rather than a default.
paper.rtp: The study describes recovery practice in healthy collegiate athletes after training and competition, and does not address injury rehabilitation or return to sport. It cannot inform return-to-play decisions. Its beliefs-versus-use findings describe what athletes do, not whether a modality helps an injured athlete recover.

records.sourceFile: Relative Rest Correlates to Winning Percentage in 2022 National Football League Season - A Preliminary Study.pdf

paper.citation: Jajtner, A. R., Pinzone, A. G., Abu-Amara, Y., Gant, R. W., Rivera, J., Tagesen, E. C., et al. Relative Rest Correlates to Winning Percentage in 2022 National Football League Season: A Preliminary Study. International Journal of Strength and Conditioning. 2025.
paper.abstract: The authors examined whether season-average relative rest (the difference in days of rest between a team and its opponent in each game) relates to winning percentage across the 2022 NFL regular season. A significant positive correlation was found, and teams that won more often or made the playoffs had higher average relative rest.
paper.tldr: In the 2022 NFL season, teams that had more rest than their opponents, on average, won a larger share of games. The link is a single-season correlation, so it describes schedule context rather than a cause.
paper.methods: All 271 regular-season games of 2022 were analysed from public schedule data. Rest intervals were calculated per team per game, relative rest was averaged over the season, and it was correlated with winning percentage. Teams were split into thirds by relative rest and compared with ANOVA, and winning and playoff teams were compared with independent t-tests.
paper.findings: Season relative rest correlated positively with winning percentage (r = 0.338, p = 0.029), accounting for about 11.4% of the variance. Winning teams (mean relative rest 0.183) and playoff teams (0.206) had higher relative rest than losing teams (-0.175) and non-playoff teams (-0.153), both p = 0.022, with moderate effect sizes (d about 0.71). Winning percentage did not differ between the high, middle and low relative-rest groups (p = 0.133).
paper.limitations: Only one season was studied, so results may not hold in other years. The analysis is team-level and correlational. It did not include travel, time-zone change, sleep, training load, injuries or individual players. The three-group comparison of winning percentage was not significant.
paper.practicalImplications: Relative rest across a season was associated with winning. Coaches could look at rest disadvantage when planning load management in the weeks a team has less rest than its opponent, as the authors suggest. The study does not show that managing rest changes results.
paper.athleteDev: Use relative rest as one schedule factor when planning training load and recovery in weeks when a team has less rest than its opponent. Do not treat the finding as evidence that a specific load plan improves performance, because the study did not measure training or athlete outcomes.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It has no injury, rehabilitation, or individual athlete return data, and its team-level results should not be applied to decisions about a single athlete.
